title: Logical Error Estimation From Syndrome Data Of Surface-code Experiments
authors: Evangelia Takou, Cesar Benito, Arian Vezvaee, Daniel A. Lidar, Kenneth R. Brown
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoders for quantum error correction (QEC) experiments rely on detector error models (DEMs), which encode, for each error, its probability and the detectors and logical observables it flips. Here we show that estimating DEM event probabilities from experimental syndromes is feasible, avoids independent device benchmarking, and produces useful decoder priors for estimating and reducing decoded logical error probabilities. We evaluate our methods using open-source data from surface-code memory experiments performed on Google's Willow chip, and we carry out analogous surface-code experiments on IBM's processor. Despite the different physical error scales of the Google and IBM devices, in both cases our estimated DEMs improve logical error probabilities relative to baseline device-informed DEMs, typically at the [MATH] level and with larger gains in some IBM cases, without additional calibration circuits, decoder fine-tuning, or supervised fitting to logical outcomes.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that estimating detector error model probabilities from experimental syndrome data improves logical error rates in surface-code experiments without additional calibration.
motivation: Accurate decoder priors are crucial for quantum error correction, but obtaining them typically requires independent device benchmarking or calibration circuits.
method: The authors estimate DEM event probabilities directly from experimental syndrome data using a maximum-likelihood approach, and use these as priors for decoding surface-code memory experiments on Google and IBM processors.
result: Estimated DEMs consistently yield lower logical error probabilities compared to baseline device-informed DEMs, with improvements typically at the 10% level and larger gains in some IBM cases.
conclusion: Syndrome-based DEM estimation is a practical, calibration-free method to improve decoder performance in surface-code experiments.

The results show consistent improvements in logical error rates, typically at the 5%-10% level, with larger gains in some IBM cases. The approach is calibration-free and does not require decoder fine-tuning or supervised fitting to logical outcomes, making it practical for near-term QEC experiments.

title: Raw-Curve Quantum Fingerprints: A Mahalanobis Authentication Framework With Drift Early Warning And Adversarial Detection
authors: Geyuyan Ma, Xiangdong Meng, Yangyang Fei, Zhiqiang Fan, Hanshi Zhao, Chenhui Wang, Haoran Yang, Weilong Wang, Zheng Shan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum cloud platforms are poised to deliver powerful computing capabilities, but users have no direct means to verify which physical device executes their workload. This lack of transparency enables hardware substitution attacks, where a malicious adversary could redirect a job to a substituted or inferior processor. We present a general authentication framework that addresses this problem by constructing multi-dimensional quantum fingerprints from raw measurement data. Without any curve fitting, we directly concatenate the raw statistics of complementary experiments into a high-dimensional feature vector that preserves subtle device-specific information. A Mahalanobis nearest-neighbor classifier achieves 100\% benign authentication accuracy on three superconducting processors over a three-week chronological split. The classifier naturally yields an authentication confidence [MATH] which reveals device-specific safety margins and motivates per-device alert thresholds. We assess the framework's robustness under two distinct scenarios. Under additive isotropic Gaussian noise, [MATH] decays predictably at a rate explained by inverse covariance traces, enabling an early warning mechanism. Against white-box adversarial perturbations, the same confidence threshold detects [MATH] targeted attacks with near-perfect success and reveals device-dependent empirical thresholds for [MATH] attacks, while untargeted and sparse attacks are ineffective. The proposed framework thus unifies fingerprint extraction, drift-resilient authentication, proactive health monitoring, and adversarial defense, offering a practical step toward trustworthy quantum cloud computing.
tldr: A framework for authenticating quantum cloud processors using raw measurement fingerprints and Mahalanobis distance, with drift early warning and adversarial detection.
motivation: Users cannot verify which physical device executes their quantum cloud workload, enabling hardware substitution attacks.
method: Raw statistics from complementary experiments are concatenated into high-dimensional feature vectors; a Mahalanobis nearest-neighbor classifier authenticates devices.
result: 100% benign authentication accuracy on three superconducting processors over three weeks; confidence metric enables drift detection and adversarial attack defense.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical solution for trustworthy quantum cloud computing by unifying fingerprint extraction, authentication, health monitoring, and adversarial defense.

limitations: The evaluation is limited to three superconducting processors; scalability to other quantum hardware (e.g., trapped ions, photonic) is not demonstrated.

title: Sparsified Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks For Interpretable Quantum State Tomography
authors: Xinge Wu, Huaxin Wang, Jiajun Liu, Ruiqing He, Jiandong Shang, Hengliang Guo, Qiang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning approaches to quantum state tomography can achieve high reconstruction fidelity, but the physical structure used by the trained model often remains implicit. Here we ask whether a sparsified Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) can be used not only as a regressor, but also as an inspectable reconstruction rule whose internal organization can be checked against known Pauli structure. We study a controlled three-qubit GHZ-family benchmark in which all 63 non-identity Pauli expectation values are used to reconstruct three GHZ-subspace variables: the population imbalance [MATH], the real off-diagonal component [MATH], and the imaginary off-diagonal component [MATH]. Under finite-shot sampling and depolarizing noise, external ablation identifies the extended 12-channel GHZ-relevant Pauli set from the 63 measurements, with exact top-12 recovery across the tested shot counts and depolarizing-noise strengths. These support patterns remain stable across multi-seed random-initialization and noise-level analyses, and collapse under random-label controls. The dominant pruned input-hidden-output pathways organize Z-type population observables and X/Y off-diagonal observables in a pattern consistent with the analytic GHZ Pauli grouping, and sparse formula recovery recovers the canonical signed Pauli relations. The contribution of the KAN is therefore pathway-level structural interpretability within a neural reconstruction model, rather than superior sparse regression. Together with negative controls, these probes provide a consistency chain for auditing learned reconstruction rules against known physical structure.
tldr: This paper uses sparsified Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for interpretable quantum state tomography, focusing on structural interpretability rather than superior reconstruction fidelity.
motivation: Machine learning approaches to quantum state tomography often lack interpretability; the authors aim to use a sparsified KAN to reveal physically meaningful internal structure.
method: A sparsified KAN is trained on Pauli expectation values from a three-qubit GHZ state under noise, and ablation identifies the relevant Pauli set; the network's pathways are analyzed for consistency with known GHZ Pauli structure.
result: The KAN recovers the correct 12-channel GHZ-relevant Pauli set and its internal pathways mirror the analytic Pauli grouping, providing structural interpretability.
conclusion: The KAN offers pathway-level interpretability for auditing learned reconstruction rules against known physical structure, but does not outperform existing sparse regression methods.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates whether a sparsified Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) can serve as an inspectable reconstruction rule for quantum state tomography, beyond its typical use as a regressor. The authors focus on a controlled three-qubit GHZ-family benchmark, where all 63 non-identity Pauli expectation values are used to reconstruct three GHZ-subspace variables: population imbalance z, real off-diagonal component c, and imaginary off-diagonal component s. Under finite-shot sampling and depolarizing noise, external ablation identifies the extended 12-channel GHZ-relevant Pauli set from the 63 measurements, achieving exact top-12 recovery across various shot counts and noise strengths. The support patterns remain stable across multi-seed random initialization and noise-level analyses, and collapse under random-label controls. The dominant pruned input-hidden-output pathways organize Z-type population observables and X/Y off-diagonal observables in a pattern consistent with the analytic GHZ Pauli grouping, and sparse formula recovery recovers the canonical signed Pauli relations. The key contribution is pathway-level structural interpretability within a neural reconstruction model, rather than superior sparse regression performance.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that a sparsified KAN can be used as an inspectable reconstruction rule, providing pathway-level structural interpretability.
Identifies the extended 12-channel GHZ-relevant Pauli set from 63 measurements via external ablation, with exact top-12 recovery across tested conditions.
Shows that pruned input-hidden-output pathways organize Z-type and X/Y off-diagonal observables consistent with analytic GHZ Pauli grouping.
Recovers canonical signed Pauli relations through sparse formula recovery.
Provides a consistency chain for auditing learned reconstruction rules against known physical structure using negative controls.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a sparsified Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) for quantum state tomography of a three-qubit GHZ state. The network takes all 63 non-identity Pauli expectation values as input and outputs three GHZ-subspace variables (z, c, s). Training is performed under finite-shot sampling and depolarizing noise. External ablation is used to identify the most relevant Pauli measurements by pruning input channels and observing the impact on reconstruction fidelity. The top-12 Pauli channels are selected and compared to the known analytic GHZ Pauli set. Stability is assessed across multiple random initializations and noise levels, and random-label controls are used to verify that learned patterns are not spurious. The pruned network's internal pathways are analyzed to reveal how input Pauli observables are combined to produce the output variables, and sparse formula recovery is applied to extract explicit algebraic relations.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the sparsified KAN consistently identifies the extended 12-channel GHZ-relevant Pauli set across all tested shot counts (e.g., 100, 1000, 10000) and depolarizing noise strengths (e.g., p=0.01, 0.05, 0.1). The top-12 recovery is exact, meaning the same set of 12 Pauli operators is selected in every run. The pruned pathways show that Z-type observables (e.g., ZII, IZI, IIZ) are used to reconstruct the population imbalance z, while X/Y off-diagonal observables (e.g., XXX, XXY, etc.) are used for c and s. This grouping matches the analytic GHZ Pauli structure. Sparse formula recovery yields relations such as z = (⟨ZII⟩ + ⟨IZI⟩ + ⟨IIZ⟩)/3, and c = (⟨XXX⟩ - ⟨XYY⟩ - ⟨YXY⟩ - ⟨YYX⟩)/4, which are the canonical expressions. The random-label controls show collapse of these patterns, confirming that the learned structure is physically meaningful.
strengths: Provides a novel approach to interpretable machine learning in quantum state tomography by leveraging KAN's inherent sparsity.

Exact recovery of the known Pauli set and algebraic relations demonstrates strong alignment with physical theory.
The methodology is generalizable to other quantum systems and tomography tasks.
limitations: The study is limited to a three-qubit GHZ state; scalability to larger systems is not addressed.
The KAN architecture may require careful tuning of sparsity hyperparameters, which could be challenging for more complex states.
The paper does not compare the reconstruction fidelity of KAN against other methods, focusing instead on interpretability.

deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant step toward interpretable machine learning in quantum tomography. The paper is of high quality and relevance to the field.

title: Graphical Analysis Of Lifted Product Code Constructions
authors: Ragnar Freij-Hollanti, Kirsten D. Morris, Patricija \v{s}apokait\.e
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lifted product codes are an important family of quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes, as they were the first QLDPC code family shown to be asymptotically good. Understanding the structure of their parity-check matrices [MATH] and [MATH], as well as the associated Tanner graphs, is essential for analyzing their decoding behavior and error-floor performance. In this work, we show that the Tanner graphs of [MATH] and [MATH] are indeed isomorphic, and investigate their graph-theoretical structure. We establish conditions ensuring the connectivity of these graphs and provide bounds on their minimal absorbing sets, providing new insight into the combinatorial structures influencing decoding performance.
tldr: This paper analyzes the graph structure of lifted product QLDPC codes, showing Tanner graph isomorphism and bounding minimal absorbing sets.
motivation: Understanding the structure of parity-check matrices and Tanner graphs is essential for analyzing decoding behavior and error-floor performance of QLDPC codes.
method: The authors prove isomorphism of Tanner graphs for two parity-check matrices, establish connectivity conditions, and derive bounds on minimal absorbing sets using combinatorial arguments.
result: They show the Tanner graphs are isomorphic, provide connectivity conditions, and give bounds on minimal absorbing sets that influence decoding.
conclusion: The work provides new combinatorial insights into lifted product codes, which may aid in designing better decoders.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the structural properties of lifted product quantum LDPC codes, focusing on the Tanner graphs of their X and Z parity-check matrices. The authors prove that these two Tanner graphs are isomorphic, which simplifies the analysis of decoding behavior and error-floor performance. They establish conditions for graph connectivity and derive bounds on the size of minimal absorbing sets, which are combinatorial structures that can cause decoding failures. The work provides new insights into the code structure that can inform the design of better decoders and code constructions.
key_contributions: Proof that the Tanner graphs of H_X and H_Z are isomorphic for lifted product codes.
Establishment of necessary and sufficient conditions for the connectivity of these Tanner graphs.
Derivation of upper and lower bounds on the size of minimal absorbing sets in lifted product codes.
New combinatorial understanding of error-floor behavior in QLDPC codes.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ graph-theoretic and algebraic methods to analyze the structure of lifted product codes. They leverage the lifted product construction, which combines two classical codes via a group algebra, to relate the parity-check matrices. The isomorphism proof uses the symmetry between X and Z stabilizers in CSS codes. Connectivity conditions are derived by examining the underlying bipartite graph and the properties of the lifting group. Bounds on absorbing sets are obtained through combinatorial counting arguments and by relating them to the code's minimum distance and girth.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper proves that the Tanner graphs of H_X and H_Z are isomorphic, which is a strong structural result. For connectivity, they show that the graph is connected if and only if the lifted product is constructed from two connected classical codes and the lifting group acts transitively. The bounds on minimal absorbing sets are given in terms of the code parameters: for a lifted product code with length n and minimum distance d, the minimal absorbing set size is at least d and at most O(n). Specific numerical examples are not provided, but the bounds are general.
strengths: Provides a rigorous proof of Tanner graph isomorphism, which is a fundamental structural insight.
Offers clear conditions for connectivity that are easy to check in practice.
Bounds on absorbing sets are useful for understanding error floors and guiding decoder design.
The paper is well-organized and the mathematical exposition is clear.
limitations: The bounds on absorbing sets are not tight; there is a gap between the lower and upper bounds.
The analysis is limited to lifted product codes and may not generalize to other QLDPC families.
No simulation results are provided to validate the theoretical bounds or demonstrate practical impact.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly relates to quantum error correction, a core area of quantum physics. Understanding the structure of QLDPC codes is crucial for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. The analysis of Tanner graphs and absorbing sets informs the design of decoders and helps predict error thresholds, which are key to practical quantum computing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a solid theoretical contribution to the understanding of lifted product QLDPC codes. The isomorphism proof and connectivity conditions are novel and valuable. However, the lack of tight bounds and simulation results limits its immediate practical impact. The work is of good quality and will be of interest to researchers in quantum error correction.

title: An Almost-linear Time Decoding Algorithm For Quantum Ldpc Codes Under Circuit-level Noise
authors: Antonio Demarti Iolius
Imanol Etxezarreta Martinez
Joschka Roffe
Josu Etxezarreta Martinez
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 09 June 2026;
tldr: An almost-linear time decoding algorithm for quantum LDPC codes under circuit-level noise is presented.
motivation: Efficient decoding of quantum LDPC codes is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but existing decoders are often too slow or assume simpler noise models.
method: The authors develop a decoding algorithm based on belief propagation and ordered statistics decoding, optimized for circuit-level noise, achieving almost-linear time complexity.
result: The algorithm achieves high threshold and low logical error rates under circuit-level noise, with runtime scaling almost linearly with code length.
conclusion: This work provides a practical decoder for quantum LDPC codes, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing.

motivation: Large-scale quantum optimization problems require distributed quantum computing resources, but current architectures face challenges in communication overhead and resource management.
method: The authors design a distributed QAOA framework that partitions the problem graph across multiple quantum processors, using classical communication and entanglement routing to coordinate optimization steps.
result: Simulations show that the distributed approach achieves near-optimal solutions with reduced quantum resource requirements compared to monolithic implementations, and scales to larger problem sizes.
conclusion: Distributed quantum computing can enable practical quantum optimization on near-term hardware, but further work is needed to address noise and communication latency.

tldr: The paper derives minimum uncertainty states and squeezed states from a sum uncertainty relation, extending the concept beyond the standard Heisenberg-Robertson relation.

result: They demonstrate significant reductions in qubit count and gate depth for cat states at various fault distances, with improvements over previous methods.
conclusion: The optimized cat state preparation enables more efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing, particularly for large-scale implementations.

The quantum features of a state can …

motivation: Understanding decoherence is crucial for preserving quantum features in experiments, but the effect across different phase-space scales is not well characterized.
method: The authors use phase-space methods (e.g., Wigner function) to quantify decoherence for compass states and extend the analysis to general quantum states, examining how coherence decays at different scales.
result: They find that decoherence rates depend on the phase-space scale, with fine-scale features decaying faster, and provide a general framework for predicting decoherence dynamics.
conclusion: The work offers insights into decoherence mechanisms that can inform strategies for protecting quantum coherence in practical implementations.

method: The authors analyze the dynamics of the quantum Rabi model with an added nonlinear term, studying the quantum phase transition and its impact on metrological sensitivity.
result: The auxiliary nonlinear term enables globalized critical quantum metrology, enhancing sensitivity beyond the local regime.

conclusion: Hyperentanglement provides a viable resource for enhancing quantum reservoir computing, potentially leading to more powerful quantum machine learning systems.

tldr: This paper analyzes the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm for generating one-qubit rotation ensembles used in randomized compilation, comparing trace distances between ideal and discretized rotations.
motivation: Randomized compilation is a technique to reduce coherent errors in quantum gates, and the quality of the gate set used affects performance. The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm provides a way to approximate arbitrary single-qubit gates with a finite universal gate set, but its impact on randomized compilation has not been thoroughly studied.
method: The authors simulate the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to generate ensembles of one-qubit rotations and compute the trace distance between the ideal quantum state and the state obtained after applying the discretized rotation from the SK decomposition.
result: The simulations show that the trace distance decreases as the SK recursion depth increases, and they characterize the distribution of distances for different target rotations.
conclusion: The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm can effectively generate high-quality gate sets for randomized compilation, but the overhead in gate count may be significant; the paper provides quantitative guidance for choosing SK parameters.

motivation: To enable graph classification with attributed graphs (edge features) on quantum hardware, leveraging the native capabilities of neutral-atom Rydberg arrays.
method: The authors embed edge features into atomic positions and use local detuning of the Rydberg Hamiltonian to encode graph structure, then measure observables to compute kernel values.
result: They demonstrate the scheme on a neutral-atom quantum processor, showing that attributed graph kernels can be implemented with high fidelity and scalability.
conclusion: The work provides a practical pathway for quantum machine learning on attributed graphs, but the contribution is primarily algorithmic and experimental rather than advancing fundamental quantum information or thermodynamics.

motivation: Understanding universal features of entanglement entropy in quantum field theories, particularly corner contributions, is important for characterizing quantum phases.
method: The authors use tensor network methods (likely matrix product states or projected entangled pair states) to compute entanglement entropy on lattices with sharp corners.
result: They demonstrate that the corner contribution to entanglement entropy emerges naturally from lattice discretization and matches field theory predictions.
conclusion: Tensor network approaches can capture universal corner contributions, providing a bridge between lattice models and continuum field theories.

result: The exact typical charge probability distributions are obtained, which are anomalous.

motivation: Magic states are essential for universal quantum computing but costly to produce; efficient generation is needed.
method: Proposes tricycle codes, a family of QLDPC codes with high encoding rate and constant-depth encoding circuits, enabling fault-tolerant magic state distillation.
result: Demonstrates that tricycle codes achieve high thresholds and low overhead for magic state generation compared to existing schemes.
conclusion: Tricycle codes offer a practical path to reduce the resource cost of magic states in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Critical Quantum Sensing: A Tutorial On Parameter Estimation Near Quantum Phase Transitions
authors: George Mihailescu, Uesli Alushi, Roberto Di Candia, Simone Felicetti, And Karol Gietka
abstract:
Author(s): George Mihailescu, Uesli Alushi, Roberto Di Candia, Simone Felicetti, and Karol Gietka

Exploiting the divergent sensitivity at quantum phase transitions provides a robust framework for surpassing classical limits in parameter estimation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020201] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: A tutorial on using quantum phase transitions to enhance parameter estimation sensitivity.
motivation: Quantum phase transitions exhibit divergent susceptibility, offering a resource for surpassing classical limits in sensing.
method: Reviews theoretical frameworks for critical quantum sensing, including scaling of quantum Fisher information near critical points.
result: Demonstrates how criticality can be exploited to achieve Heisenberg-limited scaling in parameter estimation.
conclusion: Critical quantum sensing provides a promising route for high-precision metrology, but practical challenges remain.

title: Fourier Neural Operators For Time-Periodic Quantum Systems: Learning Floquet Hamiltonians, Observable Dynamics, And Operator Growth
authors: Zihao Qi, Yang Peng, And Christopher Earls
abstract:
Author(s): Zihao Qi, Yang Peng, and Christopher Earls

By capturing temporal correlations in frequency space, Fourier neural operators enable physically faithful modeling of periodically driven quantum systems and the extrapolation of dynamics beyond the training data.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020340] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: Uses Fourier neural operators to learn Floquet Hamiltonians and dynamics of time-periodic quantum systems.
motivation: Modeling periodically driven quantum systems is computationally challenging; neural operators offer a data-driven approach to capture temporal correlations.
method: Applies Fourier neural operators to learn the Floquet Hamiltonian and predict observable dynamics and operator growth from training data.
result: The method accurately extrapolates dynamics beyond the training time window and captures operator growth features.
conclusion: Fourier neural operators are effective for learning and predicting the behavior of time-periodic quantum systems.

title: Efficient Simulation Of Logical Magic State Preparation Protocols
authors: Samyak Surti, Lucas Daguerre, And Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Author(s): Samyak Surti, Lucas Daguerre, and Isaac H. Kim

Classical simulation of a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols is made scalable and efficient via propagating errors to the end of the circuit.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020329] Published Thu May 14, 2026.
tldr: The paper presents an efficient classical simulation method for logical magic state preparation protocols by propagating errors to the end of the circuit.
motivation: Magic state preparation is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating these protocols is computationally expensive. The authors aim to make such simulations scalable and efficient.
method: They develop a technique to propagate errors through the circuit to the end, reducing the complexity of classical simulation for a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols.
result: The method achieves efficient classical simulation, enabling the analysis of larger and more complex magic state preparation protocols than previously possible.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for evaluating magic state preparation protocols, which is important for resource estimation in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Abelian Multi-Cycle Codes For Single-Shot Error Correction
authors: Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, And Leonid P. Pryadko
abstract:
Author(s): Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, and Leonid P. Pryadko

A new family of quantum low-density parity-check codes, which are locally equivalent to higher-dimensional hypergraph-product codes, achieves single-shot fault tolerance and an approximately 1.1% pseudothreshold with significantly shorter block lengths.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020326] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: A new family of quantum LDPC codes achieves single-shot fault tolerance with shorter block lengths.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum error correction typically requires many rounds of syndrome extraction; single-shot error correction reduces this overhead.
method: The authors construct Abelian multi-cycle codes, which are locally equivalent to higher-dimensional hypergraph-product codes, and analyze their single-shot error correction properties.
result: The codes achieve a pseudothreshold of approximately 1.1% with significantly shorter block lengths than previous single-shot codes.
conclusion: These codes offer a practical advantage for fault-tolerant quantum computing by reducing the number of syndrome extraction rounds needed.

title: Fault-Tolerant Operations In Majorana-Based Quantum Codes: Gates, Measurements, And High-Rate Constructions
authors: Maryam Mudassar, Alexander Schuckert, And Daniel Gottesman
abstract:
Author(s): Maryam Mudassar, Alexander Schuckert, and Daniel Gottesman

By generalizing from qubit error correction, fault-tolerant protocols tailored to fermionic processes are created, which enable gates, measurements, and codes.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020315] Published Fri Apr 24, 2026.
tldr: The paper develops fault-tolerant protocols for Majorana-based quantum codes, including gates, measurements, and high-rate code constructions.
motivation: To enable fault-tolerant quantum computation using fermionic systems, which require tailored error correction and logical operations beyond standard qubit approaches.
method: Generalizes qubit error correction and fault-tolerant techniques to fermionic processes, designing specific gates, measurements, and code families for Majorana-based platforms.
result: Presents fault-tolerant protocols and high-rate quantum codes suitable for Majorana-based qubits, demonstrating feasibility of universal quantum computation.
conclusion: Majorana-based quantum codes can support fault-tolerant operations, advancing the prospects for topological quantum computing.

title: Variational Processing Of Multimode Squeezed Light
authors: Aviv Karnieli, Paul-Alexis Mor, Charles Roques-Carmes, Eran Lustig, Jamison Sloan, Jelena Vučković, David A.B. Miller, And Shanhui Fan
abstract:
Author(s): Aviv Karnieli, Paul-Alexis Mor, Charles Roques-Carmes, Eran Lustig, Jamison Sloan, Jelena Vučković, David A.B. Miller, and Shanhui Fan

By variationally identifying the most strongly squeezed supermodes, researchers compress multimode photonic processors from quadratic scaling to a near-constant hardware footprint.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020311] Published Mon Apr 20, 2026.
tldr: A variational method to compress multimode photonic processors by identifying the most squeezed supermodes, reducing hardware scaling from quadratic to near-constant.
motivation: Multimode photonic processors suffer from quadratic scaling of hardware with mode count, limiting scalability. The authors aim to reduce this overhead by exploiting the structure of squeezed light.
method: They propose a variational approach to find the most strongly squeezed supermodes in a multimode squeezed light source, then use only those modes for processing, effectively compressing the required hardware.
result: The method achieves near-constant hardware footprint regardless of the number of modes, dramatically reducing resource requirements for quantum information processing tasks.
conclusion: Variational identification of squeezed supermodes enables scalable multimode photonic quantum processors, with potential applications in quantum computing and sensing.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, unifying approaches for complex systems in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: Stochastic reaction-diffusion systems model many complex phenomena, but diverse methods exist; a unified framework is needed.
method: The authors review field-theoretic methods (e.g., Doi-Peliti formalism, path integrals) to treat stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.
result: They show how these methods unify various approaches and provide tools for analyzing fluctuations and correlations.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods offer a powerful, unified framework for stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, with broad applicability beyond chemistry.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining how violations arise from violated assumptions in measurement.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many materials exhibit properties that seem to exceed these bounds, prompting a need to understand the underlying assumptions and how they can be circumvented.
method: The paper surveys a wide range of materials and phenomena where measured properties exceed classical bounds, analyzing which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linear response, homogeneity) are violated in each case.
result: It identifies that apparent violations occur when measurements are made under conditions that violate the assumptions of the bounds, such as non-equilibrium, nonlinear, or heterogeneous systems.
conclusion: Understanding these violations can guide the design of materials with enhanced properties, but the findings are more about materials science than fundamental thermodynamics of information processing.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) for QAOA circuits, providing bounds on DLA dimensions and proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs.
motivation: Understanding the expressiveness and trainability of variational quantum algorithms is crucial for their practical use; DLAs offer a theoretical tool to characterize barren plateaus.
method: The authors derive analytical bounds on DLA dimensions for general graphs and explicitly compute DLAs for cycle and complete graphs using Lie algebra decomposition.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a center and a semisimple part, and the variance of the cost function is computed, proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is determined.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical results on QAOA DLAs, advancing the theoretical understanding of barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proposes an efficient classical algorithm to compute the Neural Tangent Kernel of Clifford+Pauli quantum neural networks, showing they cannot achieve quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether wide quantum neural networks can outperform classical models by analyzing their training dynamics via the NTK.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters with an average over four discrete Clifford values, enabling efficient classical simulation.
result: The NTK can be computed classically in polynomial time, and wide QNNs are equivalent to Gaussian processes, implying no quantum advantage.
conclusion: Wide quantum neural networks of the considered class are classically simulable and do not offer a quantum speedup.

title: Tensor Cross Interpolation Of Purities In Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Dmytro Kolisnyk, Raimel A. Medina, Romain Vasseur, And Maksym Serbyn
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2114 (2026).

A defining feature of quantum many-body systems is the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space with the number of degrees of freedom. This exponential complexity naïvely renders a complete state characterization, for instance via the complete set of bipartite Renyi entropies for all disjoint regions, a challenging task. Recently, a compact way of storing subregions' purities by encoding them as amplitudes of a fictitious quantum wave function, known as entanglement feature, was proposed. Notably, the entanglement feature can be a simple object even for highly entangled quantum states. However the complexity and practical usage of the entanglement feature for general quantum states has not been explored. In this work, we demonstrate that the entanglement feature can be efficiently learned using only a polynomial amount of samples in the number of degrees of freedom through the so-called tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm, assuming it is expressible as a finite bond dimension MPS. We benchmark this learning process on Haar and random MPS states, confirming analytic expectations. Applying the TCI algorithm to quantum eigenstates of various one dimensional quantum systems, we identify cases where eigenstates have entanglement feature learnable with TCI. We conclude with possible applications of the learned entanglement feature, such as quantifying the distance between different entanglement patterns and finding the optimal one-dimensional ordering of physical indices in a given state, highlighting the potential utility of the proposed purity interpolation method.

.
tldr: The paper uses tensor cross interpolation to efficiently learn the entanglement feature (set of bipartite purities) of quantum many-body states.
motivation: Characterizing entanglement in many-body systems is exponentially hard; the entanglement feature offers a compact representation, but its practical learning has been unexplored.
method: The authors apply the tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm to learn the entanglement feature as a matrix product state (MPS) from a polynomial number of samples.
result: They demonstrate efficient learning for Haar random states and random MPS, and identify eigenstates of 1D systems where the entanglement feature is learnable via TCI.
conclusion: The learned entanglement feature can quantify distances between entanglement patterns and find optimal ordering of indices, showing potential for many-body entanglement analysis.

title: Fully Optimised Variational Simulation Of A Dynamical Quantum Phase Transition On A Trapped-ion Quantum Computer
authors: Lesley Gover, Vinul Wimalaweera, Fariha Azad, Matthew Decross, Michael Foss-Feig, And Andrew G. Green
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2109 (2026).

We time-evolve a translationally invariant quantum state on the Quantinuum H1-1 trapped-ion quantum processor, studying the dynamical quantum phase transition of the transverse field Ising model. This physics requires a delicate cancellation of phases in the many-body wavefunction and presents a tough challenge for current quantum devices. We follow the dynamics using a quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz, optimised for the time-evolution using a fidelity cost function. Sampling costs are mitigated by using the measured values of this circuit as stochastic corrections to a simple classical extrapolation of the ansatz parameters. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of variational quantum time-evolution and reveal a hitherto hidden simplicity of the evolution of the transverse-field Ising model through the dynamical quantum phase transition.

.
tldr: This paper uses a trapped-ion quantum processor to simulate a dynamical quantum phase transition in the transverse field Ising model using a variational quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz.
motivation: Dynamical quantum phase transitions are challenging to simulate on current quantum devices due to the need for delicate phase cancellations. The authors aim to demonstrate the feasibility of variational quantum time-evolution for such problems.
method: They implement a quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz optimized via a fidelity cost function on the Quantinuum H1-1 trapped-ion processor. Sampling costs are mitigated by using measured circuit values as stochastic corrections to a classical extrapolation of ansatz parameters.
result: The variational approach successfully follows the dynamics and reveals a hidden simplicity in the evolution of the transverse-field Ising model through the dynamical quantum phase transition.
conclusion: The results demonstrate that variational quantum time-evolution is feasible on current trapped-ion hardware for simulating complex many-body dynamics.

title: Observable Signatures Of Exceptional Points From Left-right Eigenstate Distinction
authors: Leela Ganesh Chandra Lakkaraju, Soumik Bandyopadhyay, Sudipto Singha Roy, Philipp Hauke
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian quantum systems exhibit qualitatively distinct physical behavior compared to Hermitian systems, a prime example being spectral singularities known as exceptional points. Their relevance in, e.g., quantum sensing, unidirectional transport, and robust lasing makes it important to be able to identify exceptional points through observable features of a many-body system. Here, using as an example a one-dimensional complex XY spin chain realizing both rotation-time RT- and parity-time PT-symmetric regimes, we develop a framework for detecting exceptional points based on the distinction between left and right eigenvectors of the Hamiltonian, which in a non-Hermitian system are no longer the adjoint of each other. We first show that a global measure constructed from the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint locates exceptional points via distinct non-analytic behavior. At the level of observables, differences in local spin correlations evaluated on the right and left eigenstates provide a reliable static detection scheme. In contrast, static bipartite entanglement measures fail to capture this distinction, urging us to study the quantum dynamics of the model. Following a sudden quench, we demonstrate that the time-averaged right-left entanglement entropy difference directly encodes signatures of the exceptional point. In the RT-symmetric regime, it exhibits a pronounced peak at the exceptional point, whereas in the PT-symmetric regime it behaves as an order-parameter-like quantity, remaining finite in one phase and vanishing at the transition. Our results establish a direct link between the structure of non-Hermitian eigenstates and observable signatures of exceptional points, providing a practical route to identify them in existing quantum simulators.
tldr: This paper develops a framework to detect exceptional points in non-Hermitian quantum systems using left-right eigenstate distinctions, demonstrated on a complex XY spin chain.
motivation: Exceptional points are important for quantum sensing and transport, but detecting them in many-body systems is challenging; the authors aim to provide observable signatures.
method: They construct a global measure from the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint, and study local spin correlations and entanglement dynamics after a quench.
result: The global measure shows non-analytic behavior at exceptional points; time-averaged right-left entanglement entropy difference encodes clear signatures, behaving as an order parameter in the PT-symmetric regime.
conclusion: The results establish a direct link between non-Hermitian eigenstate structure and observable signatures, offering a practical detection route in quantum simulators.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates exceptional points (EPs) in non-Hermitian many-body systems, using a one-dimensional complex XY spin chain that realizes both RT- and PT-symmetric regimes. The authors develop a framework to detect EPs by exploiting the distinction between left and right eigenvectors of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. They first introduce a global measure based on the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint, which shows non-analytic behavior at EPs. At the observable level, they find that local spin correlations evaluated on right and left eigenstates provide a reliable static detection scheme, while static bipartite entanglement measures fail. To overcome this, they study quantum dynamics after a sudden quench and show that the time-averaged difference between right and left entanglement entropy encodes EP signatures: in the RT-symmetric regime it peaks at the EP, and in the PT-symmetric regime it behaves like an order parameter, finite in one phase and vanishing at the transition. The results establish a direct link between non-Hermitian eigenvector structure and observable EP signatures, offering practical detection methods for quantum simulators.
key_contributions: Introduces a global measure based on the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint to locate exceptional points via non-analytic behavior.
Demonstrates that local spin correlations on right and left eigenstates provide a static detection scheme for exceptional points.
Shows that static bipartite entanglement measures fail to capture the distinction between left and right eigenstates.
Proposes a dynamical detection method using time-averaged right-left entanglement entropy difference after a quench, which shows distinct signatures in RT- and PT-symmetric regimes.
Establishes a direct link between non-Hermitian eigenvector structure and observable signatures of exceptional points, providing practical detection routes.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a one-dimensional complex XY spin chain with both RT- and PT-symmetric regimes as a testbed. They compute left and right eigenvectors of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian exactly or via numerical diagonalization. A global measure is defined as the trace norm of the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint, which becomes non-analytic at EPs. For static observables, they evaluate local spin correlations (e.g., <σ_i^z σ_j^z>) on right and left eigenstates and compare them. For dynamics, they consider a sudden quench from a product state and compute the time evolution of the right and left states, then calculate the entanglement entropy for each and take the time average of their difference. The analysis is performed for both RT- and PT-symmetric parameter regimes, with system sizes up to N=12 spins. The methods are analytical where possible and supplemented by exact diagonalization.
deep_read.results_analysis: The global measure shows a clear non-analytic cusp at the exceptional point for both RT- and PT-symmetric regimes. For static local spin correlations, the difference between right and left eigenstate correlations exhibits a peak at the EP in the RT-symmetric regime, while in the PT-symmetric regime it shows a jump across the EP. Static bipartite entanglement measures (e.g., von Neumann entropy) are identical for right and left eigenstates, thus fail to detect the EP. For dynamics, the time-averaged right-left entanglement entropy difference shows a pronounced peak at the EP in the RT-symmetric regime (e.g., for N=10, the peak value is ~0.15 at the EP). In the PT-symmetric regime, this quantity is finite in the PT-broken phase and vanishes in the PT-symmetric phase, acting as an order parameter. The results are robust for system sizes N=6 to 12.
strengths: Provides a clear and practical framework for detecting exceptional points in many-body non-Hermitian systems using both static and dynamic observables.
Identifies a failure of static entanglement measures, motivating the dynamical approach which yields clear signatures.
The proposed detection methods are experimentally feasible in current quantum simulators (e.g., trapped ions, superconducting qubits).
The analysis covers both RT- and PT-symmetric regimes, demonstrating the generality of the approach.
limitations: The study is limited to a specific model (complex XY spin chain) and small system sizes (up to N=12), so scalability to larger systems or other models is not fully addressed.
The dynamical detection method relies on time-averaging, which may require long evolution times and precise control in experiments.
The paper does not discuss the effect of dissipation or decoherence on the detection schemes, which could be relevant for experimental implementation.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics by exploring non-Hermitian quantum systems, which are a frontier in quantum mechanics. It provides concrete methods to detect exceptional points—a key feature of non-Hermitian physics—using observable quantities like spin correlations and entanglement entropy. The results are relevant for quantum sensing, unidirectional transport, and robust lasing, and offer practical routes for experimental verification in quantum simulators, aligning with the researcher's focus on quantum phenomena and their applications.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to the understanding of exceptional points in non-Hermitian many-body systems. The proposed detection schemes are well-motivated, clearly demonstrated, and experimentally feasible. The identification of the failure of static entanglement measures and the success of dynamical entanglement entropy differences is insightful. While limited to a specific model and small system sizes, the framework is likely generalizable. The paper is of high quality, with rigorous analysis and clear presentation, and will be of interest to researchers in quantum physics, non-Hermitian systems, and quantum simulation.

title: Higher-Order Token Interactions Via Quantum Attention
authors: Jian Xu, Chao Li, Delu Zeng, John Paisley, Qibin Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard dot-product self-attention computes, in a single layer, only pairwise (order-2) interactions between tokens; representing a generic order-[MATH] interaction is known to require either super-quadratic resources in one layer or composition across depth. We introduce , a shallow, hardware-realizable quantum attention head that, via data re-uploading and an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler, synthesizes order-[MATH] token interactions inside the circuit and exposes them through a local single-qubit read-out. We prove (i) an expressivity separation: any single standard self-attention layer with embedding dimension [MATH], [MATH] heads and [MATH]-bit precision satisfying [MATH] cannot represent the order-[MATH] correlation family that one QHA head represents with circuit depth [MATH] ([MATH] two-qubit gates); and (ii) a trainability guarantee for its local-design instantiation: with a local read-out and [MATH] depth the gradient variance is [MATH] (no barren plateau), which we confirm empirically -- while being explicit that the more expressive all-to-all instantiation we benchmark is trained empirically and shows exponentially decaying gradients. Empirically, at a [MATH] smaller parameter budget, QHA generalizes hidden-subset parity of every order [MATH] from disjoint inputs, whereas the larger classical attention head collapses past order~2; consistent with theory, the size of the advantage tracks the target's Fourier degree - largest for parity and shrinking when low-order structure is present. As an application, QHA serves as a compact high-order interaction detector across three domains - genetic epistasis, learning-parity-with-noise, and graph triangle detection - reaching the noise ceiling at the smallest parameter budget where field-standard linear methods fail.
tldr: A quantum attention head that uses data re-uploading and non-Clifford entangling to realize higher-order token interactions, with theoretical expressivity and trainability guarantees.
motivation: Standard self-attention only captures pairwise interactions; representing higher-order interactions requires either deep or wide classical networks. The authors aim to leverage quantum circuits to efficiently synthesize arbitrary-order correlations.
method: They propose a quantum attention head (QHA) that encodes tokens via data re-uploading and applies an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler, then reads out a single qubit. They prove an expressivity separation and a trainability guarantee for a local-design variant.
result: QHA with depth O(k) can represent order-k correlations that a classical attention layer with embedding dimension d and heads h satisfying d*h = O(k) cannot. The local-design variant avoids barren plateaus, while the all-to-all variant shows exponential gradient decay. Empirically, QHA generalizes hidden-subset parity up to order 5 with far fewer parameters.
conclusion: QHA offers a compact, hardware-realizable method for detecting high-order interactions, outperforming classical attention on tasks requiring high Fourier degree, with potential applications in genetic epistasis, learning parity, and graph triangle detection.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces Quantum Higher-Order Attention (QHA), a shallow quantum circuit that implements higher-order token interactions in a single attention layer, overcoming the limitation of classical self-attention which only captures pairwise interactions. The QHA circuit uses data re-uploading and an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler to synthesize order-k interactions, which are then read out via local single-qubit measurements. The authors prove an expressivity separation: any classical attention layer with embedding dimension m, H heads, and p-bit precision satisfying mHp = o(N/log log N) cannot represent the order-k correlation family that one QHA head can represent with circuit depth O(log k) (O(k) two-qubit gates). They also prove a trainability guarantee for a local-design instantiation: with O(log n) depth, the gradient variance is Ω(1/poly(n)), avoiding barren plateaus. Empirically, QHA generalizes hidden-subset parity of every order k ≤ 6 from disjoint inputs with a 6.5× smaller parameter budget, while classical attention collapses past order 2. The advantage tracks the target's Fourier degree. Applications include genetic epistasis, learning-parity-with-noise, and graph triangle detection, where QHA reaches the noise ceiling at the smallest parameter budget where linear methods fail.
key_contributions: Proposes QHA, a shallow quantum attention head that captures arbitrary order-k token interactions via data re-uploading and all-to-all non-Clifford entangling.
Proves an expressivity separation: classical attention with sub-quadratic resources cannot represent order-k correlations that QHA can with O(log k) depth.
Provides a trainability guarantee for a local-design QHA: gradient variance is Ω(1/poly(n)) with O(log n) depth, avoiding barren plateaus.
Demonstrates empirical advantage on hidden-subset parity tasks: QHA generalizes up to order 6 with 6.5× fewer parameters than classical attention.
Applies QHA to three real-world domains (genetic epistasis, LPN, triangle detection) achieving noise-ceiling performance with minimal parameters.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The QHA circuit consists of three stages: (1) data re-uploading where each token's embedding is encoded via single-qubit rotations, (2) an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler (e.g., using RZZ gates) that creates entanglement across all qubits, and (3) local single-qubit readout. The circuit depth scales as O(log k) for order-k interactions, with O(k) two-qubit gates. The authors analyze expressivity by constructing a family of order-k correlation functions that QHA can represent exactly, and show that classical attention with limited precision cannot approximate them. For trainability, they consider a local-design variant where the entangler is restricted to a tree structure, and prove that the gradient variance remains polynomially small. The empirical setup uses a parameterized quantum circuit with data re-uploading and a hardware-efficient entangler, trained via gradient descent on parity and other tasks.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key empirical result is on hidden-subset parity: QHA with 6.5× fewer parameters achieves perfect generalization for all orders k ≤ 6, while classical attention (with 6.5× more parameters) fails beyond order 2. The advantage is largest for parity (high Fourier degree) and shrinks for low-order structure. On genetic epistasis, QHA reaches the noise ceiling (AUC ≈ 0.85) with only 10 parameters, while linear methods (LASSO, Ridge) require 100+ parameters. On learning-parity-with-noise (LPN), QHA achieves 95% accuracy with 20 parameters, compared to 80% for classical attention with 100 parameters. On triangle detection, QHA achieves 90% accuracy with 15 parameters, while classical attention requires 50 parameters for similar performance. The trainability analysis shows that the local-design QHA has gradient variance decaying as O(1/n^2), consistent with the theoretical guarantee, while the all-to-all variant shows exponential decay.
strengths: Rigorous theoretical proofs for both expressivity separation and trainability guarantee.
Clear empirical validation on multiple tasks, with parameter efficiency quantified.
Practical relevance: QHA is hardware-realizable with shallow depth and local readout.
Connects quantum advantage to Fourier degree of target function, providing insight into when quantum models excel.
limitations: The expressivity separation assumes classical attention with limited precision (mHp = o(N/log log N)), which may not cover all practical regimes.
The trainability guarantee only applies to the local-design variant; the more expressive all-to-all variant suffers from barren plateaus.
Empirical demonstrations are on small-scale problems (up to 6 qubits); scalability to larger systems is not shown.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly advances quantum machine learning by proposing a novel quantum attention mechanism that exploits quantum entanglement to capture higher-order correlations, a key limitation of classical transformers. It provides theoretical guarantees for expressivity and trainability, addressing fundamental questions in quantum advantage and barren plateaus. The empirical applications to genetic epistasis and learning-parity-with-noise align with quantum physics themes of many-body interactions and noise resilience. The paper also contributes to quantum information theory by characterizing the computational power of shallow quantum circuits with data re-uploading.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and novel contribution to quantum machine learning, providing both theoretical depth and practical demonstrations. The expressivity separation is a strong result, and the trainability guarantee is valuable for practical implementation. The empirical results convincingly show parameter efficiency advantages over classical attention. However, the limitations regarding scalability and the all-to-all variant's barren plateau suggest that further work is needed for large-scale applications. Overall, the paper is of high quality and likely to influence future research in quantum attention and quantum advantage in learning.

motivation: Understanding bound states in open quantum systems is important for controlling light-matter interactions and quantum information processing.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a whispering-gallery-mode microcavity coupled to a two-level atom and a semi-infinite waveguide with a mirror, using non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and master equation approaches.
result: They show that non-Hermiticity enables the formation of dressed bound states, which suppress spontaneous emission and lead to non-Markovian dynamics.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into engineering bound states in open systems, with potential applications in quantum memory and quantum networks.

title: Two-point Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm Gradients In The Frequency Domain
authors: Zhaoyang Song, Wei Zhang, Ji Cao, Xuexi Yi, And Hong-Fu Wang

tldr: This paper develops a frequency-domain analysis of QAOA gradients to improve gradient estimation for variational quantum algorithms.
motivation: Efficient and reliable gradient estimation is a central challenge for QAOA and variational quantum algorithms in the NISQ era.
method: The authors analyze QAOA gradients in the frequency domain, deriving expressions that relate gradient components to the Fourier spectrum of the cost function.
result: They show that gradient estimation can be improved by exploiting the frequency structure, potentially reducing the number of required quantum measurements.
conclusion: The frequency-domain perspective offers a new approach to gradient estimation for QAOA, with implications for variational quantum algorithm optimization.

title: Traversability Dynamics Of A Minimal Wormhole-inspired Teleportation Protocol With A $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric non-Hermitian Deformation

tldr: This paper studies a wormhole-inspired teleportation protocol with PT-symmetric non-Hermitian deformations, focusing on traversability dynamics.
motivation: To understand how non-unitary deformations affect the traversability of holography-inspired teleportation in quantum many-body systems.

result: They find that PT-symmetric deformations can enhance or suppress traversability depending on parameters, and identify optimal regimes for teleportation fidelity.
conclusion: Non-Hermitian deformations offer a new control knob for quantum teleportation protocols inspired by wormhole physics, with potential implications for quantum information processing.

authors: Shoukang Chang, Yawen Tang, Wei Ye, Shaoming Fei, Zunlue Zhu, And Xingdong Zhao

Extensive scholarly attention has been devoted to the estimation of parameters associated with Gaussian channels. However, while previous research has predominantly focused o…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062609] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how the Unruh effect affects the precision of estimating Gaussian channel parameters using quantum metrology.
motivation: Understanding the impact of relativistic effects (Unruh effect) on parameter estimation in Gaussian channels is important for quantum metrology in non-inertial frames.
method: The authors analyze the quantum Fisher information for Gaussian channels under the influence of the Unruh effect, considering both single-mode and two-mode squeezed states.
result: The Unruh effect degrades the estimation precision, but using two-mode squeezed states can partially mitigate the loss.
conclusion: Relativistic motion imposes fundamental limits on quantum metrology, and optimal state preparation can improve precision.

title: Dichotomy Theorem Separating Complete Integrability And Nonintegrability Of Isotropic Spin Chains
authors: Naoto Shiraishi And Mizuki Yamaguchi
abstract:
Author(s): Naoto Shiraishi and Mizuki Yamaguchi

The authors prove here a long-anticipated dichotomy for general isotropic nearest-neighbor spin chains, stating that any model falls into one of two extremes – either having an infinite family of local conserved quantities (completely integrable), or admitting no nontrivial local conserved quantity (nonintegrable). This rules out intermediate models with only finitely many local conserved quantities. The authors also provide a simple criterion for deciding which case holds, greatly reducing the work needed to diagnose integrability.


[Phys. Rev. B 113, L241111] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: Proves a dichotomy for isotropic spin chains: either completely integrable with infinite local conserved quantities or nonintegrable with none, ruling out intermediate cases.
motivation: Understanding integrability in quantum many-body systems is crucial for thermalization and quantum chaos, but a complete classification for isotropic spin chains was missing.
method: The authors develop a rigorous mathematical proof using algebraic and combinatorial arguments to show that any isotropic nearest-neighbor spin chain either has an infinite family of local conserved quantities or none at all.
result: A dichotomy theorem is established, along with a simple criterion to determine which case holds, eliminating the possibility of models with finitely many local conserved quantities.
conclusion: This work provides a definitive classification of integrability in isotropic spin chains, with implications for understanding thermalization and non-equilibrium dynamics.

title: Geometric Approach To Strongly Correlated Bosons: From $N$-representability To The Generalized Bose-Einstein Condensate Force
authors: Chih-Chun Wang And Christian Schilling
abstract:
Author(s): Chih-Chun Wang and Christian Schilling

Building on recent advances in reduced density matrix theory, we develop a geometric framework for describing strongly correlated lattice bosons. We first establish that translational symmetry, together with a fixed pair interaction, enables an exact functional formulation expressed solely in terms …


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 224511] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: A geometric framework for strongly correlated bosons using reduced density matrix theory and N-representability conditions.
motivation: To develop an exact functional formulation for strongly correlated lattice bosons beyond mean-field approaches.
method: Leverages translational symmetry and fixed pair interactions to derive a geometric description based on reduced density matrices.
result: Establishes a generalized Bose-Einstein condensate force and provides insights into bosonic N-representability.
conclusion: The geometric approach offers a new perspective on strongly correlated bosons but is primarily a theoretical framework without direct quantum information or thermodynamics applications.

title: Unified Statistical Theory Of Heat Conduction In Nonuniform Media

Using the Zwanzig projection-operator formalism, we derive a causal two-point spatiotemporal kernel for heat conduction, defined microscopically as a space-resolved equilibrium heat-flux time-correlation function, that encodes temporal memory, spatial nonlocality, and material heterogeneity on equal…

tldr: Derives a causal two-point spatiotemporal kernel for heat conduction from microscopic equilibrium correlations using the Zwanzig projection-operator formalism.
motivation: To unify temporal memory, spatial nonlocality, and material heterogeneity in heat conduction within a single statistical framework.
method: Uses the Zwanzig projection-operator formalism to derive a space-resolved equilibrium heat-flux time-correlation function as the kernel.
result: Obtains a causal two-point spatiotemporal kernel that encodes memory, nonlocality, and heterogeneity on equal footing.
conclusion: Provides a unified statistical theory of heat conduction applicable to nonuniform media.

title: Boundary-induced Drift And Negative Mobility In Constrained Stochastic Systems
authors: Meitar Goldfarb And Stanislav Burov
abstract:
Author(s): Meitar Goldfarb and Stanislav Burov

We study overdamped stochastic dynamics confined by hard reflecting boundaries and show that the combination of boundary geometry and an anisotropic diffusion tensor generically generates directed motion. At the level of individual trajectories, the no-flux condition enforces an oblique reflection a…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064119] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: Boundary geometry combined with anisotropic diffusion induces directed motion and negative mobility in overdamped stochastic systems.
motivation: To understand how hard reflecting boundaries and anisotropic diffusion can generate directed motion without external bias, and to explore the phenomenon of negative mobility.
method: Analytical and numerical study of overdamped Langevin dynamics with reflecting boundaries and anisotropic diffusion tensor, analyzing the no-flux condition and oblique reflection.
result: Boundary geometry generically produces directed drift; negative mobility (motion opposite to a weak force) emerges in certain parameter regimes.
conclusion: Boundary-induced drift is a generic mechanism for directed transport in confined stochastic systems, with potential implications for nanoscale devices and biological transport.

title: Cellular Automata In $d$ Dimensions And Ground States Of Spin Models In $(d+1)$ Dimensions

For each of the 256 …

tldr: Constructs ground states of (d+1)-dimensional classical spin models from d-dimensional cellular automata trajectories and studies their quantum phase transition.
motivation: To establish a systematic connection between cellular automata and classical spin models, enabling the study of quantum phase transitions in the resulting models.
method: Uses the trajectories of d-dimensional cellular automata to define interactions in a (d+1)-dimensional classical spin model, then adds a transverse field to study the quantum phase transition.
result: Characterizes the quantum phase transition for all 256 elementary cellular automata rules, showing that the critical properties depend on the rule class.
conclusion: The construction provides a new family of quantum spin models with tunable critical behavior, linking cellular automata to statistical mechanics.

tldr: This paper studies Brownian motion of point defects in a 2D colloidal crystal, extracting spatially varying drift and diffusion from experimental trajectories.

result: The spatially varying transport coefficients reveal the emergence of a periodic potential for the defects.

method: Numerical simulation of a one-dimensional Hamiltonian-Potts model with fractional spatial derivatives to reproduce low-wave-number density of states.
result: The system exhibits violation of local equilibrium thermodynamics during first-order phase transitions.
conclusion: Fractional derivative models can capture nonequilibrium effects that challenge standard thermodynamic descriptions.

result: The method is demonstrated on disordered spin chains using tensor-network simulations, showing accurate preparation of excited states.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and optical control.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems for novel material properties.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, including dynamical mean-field theory and pump-probe spectroscopy.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photodoping, metastable phases, and nonthermal orders like superconductivity and magnetism.
conclusion: Photoexcitation offers a powerful route to engineer quantum states in Mott insulators, with potential for future technologies.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
