Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene reveals gate-tunable ballistic spin transport, providing a mechanism for coherent spin control through spin-dependent electron optics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021029] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates ballistic spin transport and spin valve behavior in graphene using transverse magnetic focusing, a condensed matter physics result with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To achieve coherent spin control in graphene via electron optics, enabling gate-tunable ballistic spin transport.
method: Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene devices to observe spin-dependent electron trajectories.
result: Observation of gate-tunable ballistic spin transport and a spin valve effect.
conclusion: Graphene can serve as a platform for coherent spin control using electron optics, but the work is primarily a condensed matter transport study.

title: Dipolar Nematic State In Relaxor Ferroelectrics
authors: Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, And Shi Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, and Shi Liu

A nematic ordering underpins the behavior of relaxor ferroelectrics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021022] Published Wed Apr 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a dipolar nematic state in relaxor ferroelectrics, focusing on condensed matter physics without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Relaxor ferroelectrics exhibit complex ordering; understanding the dipolar nematic state may clarify their behavior.
method: The authors likely use theoretical modeling or experimental characterization to investigate the nematic ordering.
result: Identification of a dipolar nematic phase in relaxor ferroelectrics.
conclusion: The dipolar nematic state is a key feature of relaxor ferroelectrics, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: More Is Less In Unpercolated Active Solids
authors: Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, And Anton Souslov
abstract:
Author(s): Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, and Anton Souslov

By combining experiments with robotic metamaterials and theory, this work shows that increasing microscopic activity can counterintuitively cause a solid’s macroscale active response to vanish when active units are too sparse for the active forces to percolate through the structure.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021012] Published Mon Apr 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies active solids where increasing microscopic activity can suppress macroscopic response due to lack of percolation.
motivation: To understand how sparse active units affect the collective mechanical response of active solids.
method: Combines robotic metamaterial experiments with theoretical modeling to probe the percolation of active forces.
result: Increasing activity can lead to a vanishing macroscopic response when active units are too sparse to percolate.
conclusion: The phenomenon 'more is less' arises from the interplay between activity and percolation in active solids.

title: Physics-Based Factorized Machine Learning For Predicting Ionic Dielectric Tensors
authors: Atsushi Takigawa, Shin Kiyohara, And Yu Kumagai
abstract:
Author(s): Atsushi Takigawa, Shin Kiyohara, and Yu Kumagai

A machine-learning methodology helps screen thousands of candidate oxides to identify materials with excellent dielectric properties.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021006] Published Tue Apr 07, 2026.
tldr: A machine learning method predicts ionic dielectric tensors of oxides using physics-based factorization.
motivation: To accelerate the discovery of materials with excellent dielectric properties for technological applications.
method: A factorized machine learning model that incorporates physical constraints to predict dielectric tensors from crystal structure data.
result: The method successfully screens thousands of candidate oxides and identifies promising materials with high dielectric constants.
conclusion: Physics-based machine learning can efficiently predict dielectric properties, aiding materials discovery.

title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithms For The Jones Polynomial
authors: Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew Decross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, And Konstantinos Meichanetzidis
abstract:
Author(s): Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew DeCross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, and Konstantinos Meichanetzidis

A comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial is shown to serve as a benchmark for quantum computers and yield new insights into potential quantum advantage.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020355] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial, serving as a benchmark for quantum computers.
motivation: The Jones polynomial is a topological invariant that is hard to compute classically, making it a candidate for quantum advantage. The authors aim to demonstrate an end-to-end quantum algorithm that can be executed on near-term devices.
method: The paper designs a complete pipeline from state preparation to measurement, using a quantum circuit that implements a unitary representation of the braid group. It includes error mitigation and resource estimation for execution on trapped-ion and superconducting qubit platforms.
result: The algorithm is successfully implemented on a trapped-ion quantum processor, showing agreement with classical simulations for small knot instances. Resource estimates suggest that larger instances could outperform classical methods.
conclusion: The work establishes the Jones polynomial as a practical benchmark for quantum computers and provides insights into the resources required for quantum advantage in topological computation.

title: Photon Catalysis For General Multimode Multi-Photon Quantum State Preparation
authors: Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, And Massimo Frigerio
abstract:
Author(s): Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, and Massimo Frigerio

Using a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition, every photonic state can be prepared with realistic experimental tools and a predictable number of steps.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020323] Published Wed May 06, 2026.
tldr: A method for preparing arbitrary photonic states using symmetric tensor decomposition and photon catalysis.
motivation: Efficient preparation of complex photonic states is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing methods are often limited to specific states or require many resources.
method: The authors propose a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition to decompose any target photonic state into a sequence of photon catalysis operations, which are experimentally feasible.
result: They show that any multimode multi-photon state can be prepared with a predictable number of steps using realistic experimental tools.
conclusion: The work provides a general and resource-efficient framework for photonic state preparation, advancing photonic quantum computing and quantum optics.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications, including topology, quantum dynamics, and spintronics.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism, which has challenged established theories and opened new directions.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes experimental and theoretical results on 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: The review covers ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and multiferroics.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving with expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology, with potential for applications.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from condensed matter physics.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic states including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and may lead to new electronic states.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: Spin glasses are a model system for complex disordered systems, and understanding their dynamics has broad applications.
method: The review synthesizes experimental results, theoretical models, and large-scale numerical simulations.
result: Highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation in advancing the field.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich area for future research, with implications for many physical systems.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on material candidates and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in candidate materials, discussing their magnetic properties and topological features.
result: Highlights key materials such as α-RuCl3 and their chiral edge modes, but does not present new experimental or theoretical results.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids remain an active area of research with many open questions, and the review serves as a guide for future work.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key photophysical process affecting the efficiency of light-emitting devices and solar energy conversion, yet its theoretical description remains challenging.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models for internal conversion, including nonadiabatic dynamics, Fermi's golden rule, and mixed quantum-classical approaches.
result: The review summarizes the strengths and limitations of current methods and identifies open challenges in accurately modeling internal conversion in complex systems.
conclusion: Improved theoretical methods are needed to better understand and control internal conversion for applications in photonics and energy harvesting.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review of quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, covering formation interactions and quantum features.
motivation: To survey quantum-mechanical properties of skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion quantum mechanics, including quantum tunneling and entanglement.
result: Summarizes current understanding of quantum skyrmion behavior and identifies open questions.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmionics is an emerging field with potential for future quantum technologies, but remains largely exploratory.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the Standard Model, including their possible mediation by exotic bosons and implications for dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to probe fundamental symmetries through spin-dependent interactions beyond the Standard Model.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent exotic interactions and summarizes experimental searches using various techniques such as atomic magnetometry, torsion balances, and precision spectroscopy.
result: The review catalogs constraints on coupling constants and interaction ranges for various exotic boson mediators, highlighting the most sensitive experimental bounds.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, but no definitive evidence has been found; further improvements in experimental sensitivity are needed.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: A review of synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries such as fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions, focusing on simulation of condensed matter and gravity phenomena.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in exotic geometries that are difficult to realize in natural materials, enabling simulation of topological phenomena and models of gravity.
method: The paper surveys experimental and theoretical approaches for implementing fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems.
result: It summarizes progress in realizing synthetic geometries and discusses emergent phenomena like topological states and analogies to gravity.
conclusion: Synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries is a rapidly growing field with potential for simulating fundamental physics, but it is not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: This paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to the lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of the wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) satisfying the Pauli principle and a variable bosonic part.
result: A benchmark lithium wave function with hundreds of basis functions is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five of which are numerically significant.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in finding robust entangled states.

title: Hidden Time-nonlocal Floquet Symmetries
authors: Sigmund Kohler And Jesús Casado-Pascual
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2112 (2026).

We investigate the Floquet spectrum of a detuned, driven two-level system and show that it exhibits exact quasienergy crossings when the detuning is an integer multiple of the energy quantum of the driving field. This behavior can be explained by a hidden time-nonlocal parity, which allows the Floquet modes to be classified as even or odd. Then a generic feature is the emergence of exact crossings between quasienergies of different parity. A constructive proof of the existence of the symmetry is based on a scalar recurrence relation. Moreover, we present a general scheme for its numerical computation, which can be applied to models beyond the two-level system. Analytical results are illustrated with numerical data.

.
tldr: The paper studies hidden time-nonlocal Floquet symmetries in driven two-level systems, explaining exact quasienergy crossings via a parity classification.
motivation: To understand the origin of exact quasienergy crossings in detuned driven two-level systems, which are not explained by standard Floquet theory.
method: Analytical derivation using a scalar recurrence relation and numerical computation of the symmetry operator.
result: Exact quasienergy crossings occur when detuning is an integer multiple of the driving quantum; these are classified by a hidden time-nonlocal parity symmetry.
conclusion: The hidden symmetry provides a general framework for understanding level crossings in Floquet systems beyond the two-level model.

title: Anisotropic Fluorescence Signals Retarded Dipole-dipole Interactions In A Thermal Atomic Cloud
authors: Vyacheslav Shatokhin, Friedemann Landmesser, Mario Niebuhr, Frank Stienkemeier, Andreas Buchleitner And Lukas Bruder
abstract: We experimentally observe and theoretically explain anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals in the fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapours, at room temperature and particle densities . We identify the retarded part of the geometrically fully resolved inter-atomic, resonant dipole-dipole interaction as the crucial ingredient to theoretically reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
tldr: Experimental and theoretical study of anisotropic fluorescence signals from thermal atomic vapors due to retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: To understand the role of retarded dipole-dipole interactions in collective fluorescence from thermal atomic clouds.
method: Experimental observation of multiple quantum coherence signals in potassium vapor fluorescence combined with theoretical modeling including retarded interactions.
result: Retarded part of the dipole-dipole interaction is essential to reproduce the anisotropic features in the experimental spectra.
conclusion: Retarded interactions must be considered for accurate description of fluorescence from dense thermal atomic ensembles.

title: Construction Of near-Γ Multiple Chiral Exceptional Points In Momentum Space Of Photonic Crystal Slabs
authors: Jingyu Zhang, Yang Gao, Tianfu Ma, Wenjia Li, Weimin Ye And Jianlong Liu
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) in optical systems have attracted considerable attention because of their nontrivial topological properties and unusual physical effects. Among them, scattering EPs are particularly appealing for describing chiral response through the scattering matrix. Photonic crystal slabs offer a versatile platform for studying chiral scattering EPs in momentum space, where their topological evolution can be conveniently accessed and engineered. In this work, a convenient approach is presented for achieving chiral scattering EPs near the Γ point by exploiting the topological evolution properties in the momentum space of photonic crystal slabs. By varying the structural parameters of the photonic crystal slabs, multiple chiral EPs are identified near the Γ point, with their evolution and annihilation processes systematically analyzed. Furthermore, the pronounced transmission asymmetry observed near the EP enables polarization conversion from linear to circular, functioning as a quarter-wave plate. This approach provides a straightforward method for realizing and controlling chiral EPs in momentum space, thereby expanding the potential for practical applications in optical metadevices.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to create and control chiral exceptional points in photonic crystal slabs for polarization conversion.
motivation: Exceptional points in optical systems have topological properties and unusual effects; the goal is to achieve chiral scattering EPs near the Γ point in photonic crystal slabs.
method: By varying structural parameters of photonic crystal slabs, multiple chiral EPs are identified and their topological evolution is analyzed.
result: Multiple chiral EPs are realized near the Γ point, and transmission asymmetry enables linear-to-circular polarization conversion.
conclusion: The approach provides a straightforward method for controlling chiral EPs in momentum space, expanding applications in optical metadevices.

title: Nonreciprocal Electrical Transport In Emerging Noncentrosymmetric Systems: From Hidden Symmetry To Functional Devices
authors: Shengyao Li, Zherui Yang, Xueyan Wang, Kian Ping Loh And X Renshaw Wang
abstract: Contrary to the reciprocal electrical transport constrained by the Onsager relations, nonreciprocal electrical transport arises in noncentrosymmetric systems where the resistance depends on the direction of current flow or external stimuli such as a magnetic field. Governed by symmetry-dependent charge dynamics, these responses appear as nonreciprocal charge transport (NCT) in the longitudinal direction and the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in the transverse direction. Recent theoretical advances have expanded the range of mechanisms and material platforms capable of hosting nonreciprocal signals, revealing the role of hidden band-geometric properties. In parallel, experimental developments have exploited these effects for practical devices, offering promising alternatives to semiconductor-based rectifiers and wireless components, with advantages in broadband operation, ultrafast response, and high energy efficiency. In this review, we summarize electrical measurement techniques and characteristic transport signatures for identifying nonreciprocal phenomena and uncovering their underlying symmetry. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the fundamental mechanisms underlying NCT and NLHE, organized through representative material systems, and a subsequent examination of strategies for artificially inducing and enhancing nonreciprocity. Finally, we evaluate the technological perspectives of nonreciprocal electrical transport for electronic applications, along with key challenges and opportunities for scalable device implementation. By synthesizing current progress, this review aims to guide materials discovery and device innovation, and to inspire exploration of new symmetry settings and unconventional routes toward enhanced nonreciprocal functionalities.
tldr: A review of nonreciprocal electrical transport in noncentrosymmetric systems, focusing on symmetry-dependent charge dynamics and device applications.
motivation: To understand and harness nonreciprocal transport phenomena for novel electronic devices beyond conventional semiconductors.
method: Summarizes theoretical mechanisms (band-geometric properties) and experimental techniques for measuring nonreciprocal charge transport and nonlinear Hall effect.
result: Identifies key material platforms and strategies to induce/enhance nonreciprocity, with potential for broadband, ultrafast rectifiers.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal transport offers promising device functionalities but faces challenges in scalable implementation.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound NaMn2O4 does not magnetically order despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform electronic structure calculations and model the magnetic system as a Heisenberg model on a maple-leaf lattice, analyzing exchange pathways and thermodynamic properties.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a hierarchy of exchange couplings that nearly isolate antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage magnetic correlations and a quantum disordered ground state.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized and quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a new materials-level mechanism for frustration.

title: Hybrid Monte Carlo For Fractional Quantum Hall States
authors: Ting-Tung Wang, Ha Quang Trung, Qianhui Xu, Min Long, Bo Yang And Zi Yang Meng
abstract: We develop a hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) method to efficiently compute the physical observables from the samplings of the Laughlin and the Moore–Read (MR) wave functions of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) systems. With the advancements in methodology, including global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry, our HMC simulation is significantly faster than the widely used Metropolis Monte Carlo scheme. As a result, we can readily simulate systems with electron numbers on both disk and sphere geometries. We apply this method to investigate the topological shift obtained from the edge dipole moment, computed from the wave function density on the disk. We also numerically computed the non-Abelian braiding matrices for different braiding schemes of the MR quasiholes on the sphere. Results with much better quality compared with previous works have been achieved. With the thermodynamic limit results obtained at ease, we also discuss the future usage of our method to clarify the questions on the instability of FQH states in an ideal Chern band setting or under quantum decoherence.
tldr: Develops a hybrid Monte Carlo method for efficiently sampling fractional quantum Hall wave functions.
motivation: To overcome the computational inefficiency of standard Metropolis Monte Carlo for simulating Laughlin and Moore-Read states.
method: Combines global updates with double stereographic projection on a sphere to accelerate sampling.
result: Achieves significantly faster simulations and computes topological shift and non-Abelian braiding matrices with improved quality.
conclusion: The method enables thermodynamic limit studies and can be extended to investigate FQH state stability in Chern bands or under decoherence.

title: Kernel Embeddings And The Separation Of Measure Phenomenon
authors: Leonardo V. Santorokartik G. Waghmarevictor M. Panaretosahttps://ror.org/02s376052institute Of Mathematics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Lausanne 1015, Switzerlandbhttps://ror.org/05a28rw58department Of Mathematics, ETH Zürich, Zürich 8092, Switzerland
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 23, June 2026.
SignificanceTwo-sample testing examines whether two probability distributions on some feature space differ based on random samples. It is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, especially when feature spaces are complex. Such settings are ...
tldr: The paper uses kernel embeddings to study the separation of measures phenomenon in two-sample testing.
motivation: Two-sample testing is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, especially for complex feature spaces, and the separation of measures phenomenon is a key theoretical challenge.
method: The authors employ kernel embeddings and related functional analysis tools to characterize when two probability distributions can be distinguished via samples.
result: They provide theoretical conditions and bounds for the separation of measures using kernel methods.
conclusion: The work advances the theoretical understanding of kernel-based two-sample tests but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Layerwise Stratification And Band Reordering In Twisted Multilayer MoTe2
authors: Yueyao Fanxiao-Wei Zhangyusen Yexiaoyu Liuchong Wangkaijie Yangdi Xiaoting Caoahttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Materials Science And Engineering, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195bhttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Physics, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 23, June 2026.
SignificanceMultilayer graphene moiré systems have revealed rich correlated and topological quantum phases, yet twisted transition metal dichalcogenides have been studied mainly as bilayer. Here we show that adding more layers changes the underlying ...
tldr: This paper studies layerwise stratification and band reordering in twisted multilayer MoTe2, a condensed matter physics topic without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how adding more layers changes the electronic structure and correlated phases in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides beyond bilayers.
method: Theoretical modeling and band structure calculations for twisted multilayer MoTe2 systems.
result: Layerwise stratification and band reordering occur, altering the moiré potential and correlated phases.
conclusion: Multilayer twisted TMDs exhibit richer physics than bilayers, but the work is purely materials-focused.

title: Numerical Simulations Of The Spread From The Mean Of The Sle And Multiple Sle Dynamics
authors: Vlad Margarint Phillip Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Schramm-Loewner Evolution (SLE) describes a family of fractal curves that arise in the study of the scaling limits of many planar Statistical Physics models. These curves are modeled using the Loewner Differential Equation for the conformal maps [MATH] with a Brownian motion driver. Using Euler's Method, in the current work we performed numerical experiments to study at a fixed time the quantities [MATH] and [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the real part and [MATH] refers to the sample average. These random variables measure the 'spread' of the dynamics from the average behavior at fixed time. One of the scopes of this work is to give numerical predictions for future theoretical investigations on these quantities. When investigating these quantities in the SLE case our experiments predict that the distribution is bimodal when the dynamics started close to the origin, and it can become bell-shaped if the dynamics is started further from the origin. In the second part, we performed experiments for a Multiple SLE model whose driver is Dyson Brownian Motion. Due to singularity in the dynamics of the drivers and the many data points needed, this part is challenging from a computational perspective. In the multiple SLE case, our experiments predict that the distribution is bell-shaped in all cases. In addition, we check the changes in the distributions as we vary the parameter [MATH] in the SLE case and [MATH] in the Multiple SLE case.
tldr: Numerical simulations of Schramm-Loewner Evolution (SLE) and multiple SLE dynamics, studying the spread from the mean of the driving process.
motivation: To provide numerical predictions for the distribution of the spread from the mean in SLE and multiple SLE, which are fractal curves from statistical physics.
method: Euler's method for numerical integration of the Loewner equation with Brownian motion and Dyson Brownian motion drivers.
result: SLE spread distribution is bimodal near the origin and bell-shaped further away; multiple SLE spread is always bell-shaped.
conclusion: The numerical experiments offer predictions for future theoretical work on these quantities.

title: Time-Reversal Characteristic Modes Of Lossy Reciprocal Structures
authors: Chenbo Shi, Jin Pan, Xin Gu, Shichen Liang, Le Zuo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A time-reversal characteristic-mode decomposition is developed for reciprocal lossy electromagnetic structures. The formulation is built on a transmit--receive interpretation of reciprocity: the far-field pattern radiated by a mode determines the time-reversed incident field that is optimally matched to couple energy back into that same mode. This physical picture leads to an antilinear characteristic-mode equation whose solutions remain radiation-power orthogonal even in the presence of material loss, lossy loading, or matched absorption. As a result, the modal expansion coefficients directly represent the radiated-power contributions of the corresponding modes and avoid the singular biorthogonal normalization that may arise in nonnormal classical characteristic-mode expansions. Equivalent formulations are derived in the scattering-operator, T-matrix, and method-of-moments (MoM) frameworks, thereby connecting external wave-channel descriptions with current-space and port-excitation descriptions. The proposed modes reduce to classical characteristic modes in the lossless limit. Numerical examples involving a lossy two-sphere system and a loaded folded antenna demonstrate the radiation-power orthogonality, modal-expansion stability, and power interpretability of the proposed decomposition near exceptional points, where classical characteristic-mode expansions become singular or lose their radiated-power meaning.
tldr: Develops a time-reversal characteristic-mode decomposition for lossy reciprocal electromagnetic structures, ensuring radiation-power orthogonality even with losses.
motivation: Classical characteristic-mode expansions become singular or lose physical meaning in lossy systems; a new decomposition is needed to maintain orthogonality and power interpretability.
method: Formulates an antilinear eigenvalue problem based on a transmit-receive reciprocity interpretation, and derives equivalent formulations in scattering-operator, T-matrix, and MoM frameworks.
result: The proposed modes remain radiation-power orthogonal under loss, avoid biorthogonal normalization, and reduce to classical modes in the lossless limit; demonstrated on a lossy two-sphere system and a loaded folded antenna.
conclusion: The time-reversal characteristic-mode decomposition provides a stable and physically meaningful modal expansion for lossy reciprocal structures, useful for antenna and scattering analysis.

title: Impact Of Mode Completeness On The Accuracy Of The Coupling Theory Of Quasinormal Modes: A Strict Numerical Demonstration
authors: Can Tao, Junda Zhu, Haitao Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coupling theory of quasinormal modes (QNMs) for a coupled system of generally lossy and dispersive optical nanoresonators has been established in a rigorous manner based on the first principle of Maxwell's equations [Phys. Rev. B 102, 045430 (2020)], and can achieve superior computational efficiency and physical intuitiveness compared with full-wave numerical methods if a small set of modes can achieve a high accuracy. The QNMs suffer from an exponential divergence of far field and can form a complete basis inside but not outside the resonator. In the QNM coupling theory (QCT), it is required that the QNMs of each resonator form a complete basis in expanding the scattered field both inside and outside the resonator, which can be achieved by using regularized QNMs (RQNMs). However, a strict numerical demonstration of the impact of the mode completeness of RQNMs on the accuracy of QCT by using a virtually complete basis of RQNMs is still absent. In this paper, we will provide such a numerical demonstration along with an improvement of the QCT and some theoretical demonstrations on a rigorous incorporation of RQNMs into the QCT. The RQNMs are obtained by introducing an equivalent surface current (ESC) encircling the resonator (called ESC-RQNMs) or the perfectly matched layer (PML) surrounding the computational domain (called PML-RQNMs). The numerical example is selected as two one-dimensional resonators of slabs in the extreme coupling case of direct contact, for which a virtually complete basis of RQNMs can be solved either analytically (for ESC-RQNMs) or numerically (for PML-RQNMs). The results show that by using a virtually complete basis of RQNMs, the QCT can achieve a high accuracy in predicting both the source-free eigenmodes and the source-excited scattered field of the coupled system, which is not true if using the incomplete basis of not-regularized QNMs (i.e., physical QNMs).
tldr: This paper numerically demonstrates the impact of mode completeness on the accuracy of the coupling theory of quasinormal modes for optical nanoresonators.
motivation: The coupling theory of quasinormal modes (QNMs) can achieve high computational efficiency, but its accuracy depends on the completeness of the mode basis. A strict numerical demonstration of this dependence using a virtually complete basis was lacking.
method: The authors use regularized QNMs (RQNMs) obtained via equivalent surface current (ESC) or perfectly matched layer (PML) to form a complete basis, and test the coupling theory on two one-dimensional resonator slabs in direct contact.
result: Using a virtually complete basis of RQNMs, the coupling theory achieves high accuracy in predicting eigenmodes and scattered fields, whereas incomplete bases of not-regularized QNMs fail.
conclusion: Mode completeness is crucial for the accuracy of the quasinormal mode coupling theory, and regularized QNMs provide a complete basis that enables accurate predictions.

title: Designed-Source Reductions And A Dual-Purpose Feasibility Band For Semantic Rate-Distortion
authors: Joss Armstrong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The joint rate-distortion framework of Stavrou and Kountouris (IEEE Transactions on Communications 2023) characterises dual-fidelity tradeoffs for semantic communication on stochastic semantic sources. Many task-oriented communication systems instead use designed sources, where the semantic object is a deterministic oracle allocation [MATH] rather than a stochastic quantity given by nature. We isolate the subclass of designed sources under smooth concave utility with assumptions A1, A2 and Euclidean allocation codomain, and restrict the encoder class to deterministic common-category mappings. Within this subclass the SK exponential-tilting decoder and generalised Blahut--Arimoto iteration specialise to conditional-mean decoding and Lloyd--Max stationarity on [MATH]. When the second fidelity is a monotone single-letter distortion, the joint problem stays inside the SK admissible class; the common-category SK rate is lower-bounded by the max of the corresponding Shannon rate-distortion functions, with equality only when the common-category reconstruction is compatible and RDF-optimal. When the second fidelity is aggregate verification, the joint problem leaves the SK single-letter class and admits a constrained-design feasibility band [MATH] of width [MATH] bits in partition cardinality. The reduction and the band are scope statements on the SK apparatus, not modifications to it. A smart-grid economic-dispatch example with a non-technical-loss-detection contrast illustrates the band.
tldr: This paper studies designed-source reductions and a feasibility band for semantic rate-distortion, focusing on deterministic oracles and concave utility, which is far from the user's research interests.
motivation: To extend the joint rate-distortion framework for semantic communication to designed sources with deterministic oracles, and to characterize the feasibility region when the second fidelity is aggregate verification.
method: The paper isolates a subclass of designed sources under smooth concave utility, restricts encoders to deterministic common-category mappings, and specializes the SK exponential-tilting decoder and Blahut-Arimoto iteration to conditional-mean decoding and Lloyd-Max stationarity.
result: For monotone single-letter distortion, the joint problem stays in the SK admissible class and the common-category SK rate is lower-bounded by the max of Shannon rate-distortion functions. For aggregate verification, the problem leaves the single-letter class and yields a constrained-design feasibility band of width in partition cardinality.
conclusion: The reductions and band are scope statements on the SK apparatus, not modifications, and are illustrated with a smart-grid economic-dispatch example.

title: Quantized Stochastic Primal-Dual Methods For Distributed Optimization Under Relaxed Global Geometry
authors: Susmit Sarkar, Abhinav Raghuvanshi, Kushal Chakrabarti, Mayank Baranwal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study distributed optimization with stochastic gradients and finite-bit communication modeled by random (unbiased) quantization. We propose q-PDGD, a quantized stochastic primal-dual method, and analyze it under relaxed global geometry. Under restricted secant inequality (RSI), a constant step-size yields linear contraction to an explicit neighborhood determined by gradient noise, quantization distortion, and network connectivity, while a diminishing step-size achieves O(1/k) convergence without shared-minimizer assumptions. Under Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality, we obtain linear-to-neighborhood convergence in the same stochastic quantized setting. Our results match the best-known centralized stochastic rates in oracle complexity, and are supported by experiments demonstrating the predicted tradeoffs between quantization level, step-size choice, and graph structure.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantized stochastic primal-dual method for distributed optimization under relaxed global geometry conditions.
motivation: Distributed optimization with limited communication and stochastic gradients is important for large-scale machine learning, but existing methods often require strong convexity or restrictive assumptions.
method: The authors introduce q-PDGD, a primal-dual algorithm that uses random unbiased quantization for finite-bit communication, and analyze its convergence under restricted secant inequality (RSI) and Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) conditions.
result: Under RSI, constant step-size yields linear convergence to a neighborhood determined by noise and quantization; diminishing step-size achieves O(1/k) rate. Under PL, linear-to-neighborhood convergence is obtained. Rates match centralized stochastic optimization.
conclusion: The method effectively handles quantization and stochastic gradients in distributed settings, with theoretical guarantees matching centralized performance.

title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis Of Threshold Group Testing
authors: Remco van der Hofstad, Noela M\"uller, Connor Riddlesden
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Threshold Group Testing (TGT) problem in the noiseless and non-adaptive setting, where the objective is to exactly recover a sparse binary vector from pooled tests, using as few tests as possible. In TGT, each test applied to a subset of items returns a positive outcome if the number of 1's (defective items) in that subset meets or exceeds a specified threshold, and has a negative outcome otherwise. We investigate how the complexity of TGT compares to that of Classical Group Testing (CGT), corresponding to the special case of the threshold equal to one, and analyse the impact of increasing the threshold on the required number of tests. Our main contribution is the derivation of a sharp information-theoretic phase transition at [MATH] (non-adaptive) tests for TGT within the constant-column test design. The threshold constant [MATH] is expressed as a function of the prevalence of defectives and the threshold value. Our upper bound is derived under an analytic assumption, and we verify that this assumption is satisfied for a threshold value of 2. The value of [MATH] reveals that TGT on the constant-column design has the same information-theoretic behaviour as CGT in the low-prevalence regime. Yet, strikingly, at higher prevalences, the threshold leads to a significant reduction in the number of tests. On the other hand, we provide evidence that when the asymptotic proportion of defective items is positive, TGT actually becomes strictly harder than CGT (excluding trivial reductions).
tldr: This paper analyzes the information-theoretic complexity of threshold group testing, a combinatorial search problem, and derives sharp phase transitions for the number of tests required.
motivation: Threshold group testing generalizes classical group testing by allowing a threshold for positive test outcomes, which can reduce the number of tests in certain regimes. Understanding its fundamental limits is important for applications like medical testing or quality control.
method: The authors use information-theoretic tools (Fano's inequality, typicality) to derive lower bounds and a combinatorial algorithm (based on constant-column designs) to achieve upper bounds, establishing a sharp phase transition.
result: The threshold constant for the phase transition is expressed in terms of defect prevalence and threshold value. For low prevalence, TGT behaves like CGT, but at higher prevalences, the threshold significantly reduces the required number of tests. However, when the proportion of defectives is positive, TGT becomes strictly harder than CGT.
conclusion: Threshold group testing exhibits a rich information-theoretic landscape, with regimes where it is easier or harder than classical group testing, depending on defect prevalence.

title: Color-Rule-Function Encoding For Combinatorial Memory
authors: Alexander Khitun
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial memory is a class of memory in which information is encoded in the set of paths through a structured mesh. In this work, we introduce a systematic encoding framework, referred to as the Color-Rule-Function (CRF) approach, for representing information in combinatorial memory. The method consists of four key steps: selecting a sequence of paths in the mesh, assigning values (e.g., colors) to each cell, defining a set of rules based on the values encountered along each path, and constructing a Boolean function that determines the state of each path. . The coding procedure is illustrated by several examples. The design space scales of the CRF scale fundamentally faster compared to conventional memory. This apparent advantage arises from the use of rule-based and functional representations but is accompanied by increased hardware complexity. A possible hardware realization of the CRF framework is discussed. Importantly, the hardware overhead can be substantially reduced through the use of customized modules. The examples of the customized design are described in the text. The combination of CRF coding with customized module design may lead to a practical advantage in data storage density. According to the estimates, the data storage density may exceed Exabit per centimeter squared. A key problem that requires further investigation is related to the minimum Hamming distance between an arbitrary target bit sequence and the closest sequence realizable within the CRF framework under fixed hardware constraints.
tldr: This paper proposes a Color-Rule-Function (CRF) encoding framework for combinatorial memory, aiming to achieve extremely high data storage density.
motivation: Conventional memory technologies face scaling limits; combinatorial memory offers a potential alternative by encoding information in paths through a mesh, but lacks systematic encoding methods.
method: The CRF approach selects paths in a mesh, assigns colors to cells, defines rules based on color sequences, and constructs Boolean functions to determine path states; custom hardware modules are designed to reduce overhead.
result: The CRF framework scales fundamentally faster than conventional memory, with estimated data storage density exceeding Exabit per cm², though hardware complexity is increased.
conclusion: CRF encoding combined with customized module design may lead to practical advantages in data storage density, but further work is needed on minimum Hamming distance constraints.

title: Epistemic Fair Division Of Independence Structures
authors: Marcin Anholcer, Maciej Bartkowiak, Bart{\l}omiej Bosek, Jaros{\l}aw Grytczuk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of fair division of indivisible goods with constraints imposed by a prescribed independence structure, that is, a family of subsets of goods closed under taking subsets. As a motivating example, imagine that the goods to be divided are the available connections in a logistic, financial, or social network. The admissible bundle of goods for each agent must correspond to an acyclic set of edges, corresponding to a basic feasible solution to a linear network problem to be solved. Suppose that all agents assign the same value to each good (in the example, the network connections are equally important for every agent) and evaluate each bundle by summing the values of its goods. Is there a fair partition of the goods into such acyclic bundles? Surprisingly, the answer is yes, provided that the number of agents is at least the arboricity of [MATH], and the fairness requirement is envy-freeness up to one good (EF1). The situation becomes more mysterious when agents have arbitrary additive valuations. Our main result guarantees that, in this case, epistemic EF1 partitions always exist, which means that each agent receives an acyclic bundle for which there exists a feasible partition of the remaining goods into acyclic bundles that they do not envy up to one good. We derive this conclusion from a general result for abstract independence structures defined on the sets of goods. We also discuss connections with several conjectures concerning matroids. In particular, we prove that any Hamiltonian matroid partitionable into two independent sets admits an EF1 bipartition with respect to a common monotone valuation. We complement our results with a constructive perspective: we present explicitly two algorithms for computing the fair allocations described above. Finally, we provide illustrative examples to demonstrate these algorithms on specific instances.
tldr: This paper studies fair division of indivisible goods under independence constraints, such as acyclic subgraphs, using combinatorial and algorithmic methods.
motivation: To ensure fair allocation of goods (e.g., network connections) where each agent's bundle must be independent in a given structure, and to guarantee envy-free allocations up to one good.
method: The authors prove existence of epistemic EF1 partitions for arbitrary additive valuations using abstract independence structures, and provide explicit algorithms for computing such allocations.
result: Epistemic EF1 partitions always exist when the number of agents is at least the arboricity of the graph, and for general independence structures, epistemic EF1 partitions exist for any number of agents.
conclusion: The work establishes fundamental fairness guarantees for constrained fair division, with connections to matroid theory and algorithmic implementations.

title: Maximizing Connectivity Of Uplink RIS-Assisted Uav Networks
authors: Shahrokh Valaee Mohammed Saif
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a new approach for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) positioning and reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) partitioning to enhance connectivity of uplink RIS-assisted UAV networks. To achieve this, our approach optimizes RIS-aided link selection, RIS partitioning, and UAV positions to maximize network connectivity characterized by its Fiedler value. Meanwhile, it maintains a specific signal-to-interference plus noise ratio (SINR) constraint for user equipment (UE), which is influenced by RIS partitioning and UAV reliability. The network connectivity optimization problem is formulated using the Fiedler value subject to RIS elements allocation and SINR constraints. This problem is a computationally expensive combinatorial optimization, necessitating an efficient iterative approach. In particular, we propose a perturbation method for RIS-aided link selection, and derive a closed-form solution for RIS partitioning, with each partition tailored to optimize SINR for individual UAV. For the given RIS-aided links and RIS partitioning, we then show that the problem of UAV positioning can be formulated as a low complexity semi-definite programming (SDP) optimization problem, which can be solved using off-the-shelf CVX solvers. Our simulations show the potential gain of UAV positioning and RIS partitioning compared to the benchmark schemes from the literature.
tldr: This paper optimizes UAV positioning and RIS partitioning to maximize connectivity in uplink RIS-assisted UAV networks.
motivation: Enhancing connectivity in UAV networks is crucial for reliable communication, especially in dynamic environments.
method: The authors formulate a combinatorial optimization problem using the Fiedler value and SINR constraints, and propose an iterative approach with perturbation for link selection, closed-form RIS partitioning, and SDP for UAV positioning.
result: Simulations show that the proposed method improves network connectivity compared to benchmark schemes.
conclusion: The approach effectively optimizes UAV positions and RIS partitioning to enhance connectivity while maintaining SINR constraints.

title: A Two-Sided Sketching Algorithm For Low-rank Tensor Train Approximation
authors: Gaohang Yu, Yihao Pan, Ailun Jian, Xiaohao Cai
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tensor train (TT) decomposition is a powerful method to acquire low-rank tensors. However, the computational process is frequently obstructed by the large-scale matrix singular value decomposition (SVD). The sketching algorithm serves as an efficient data compression technique that can quickly derive low-rank matrix approximations. In this paper, we propose a randomized algorithm to obtain the TT approximation of tensors using a one-pass sketching algorithm and subspace iteration, and offer thorough error-bound and robustness analysis. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
tldr: This paper proposes a randomized algorithm for low-rank tensor train approximation using sketching and subspace iteration.
motivation: Large-scale matrix SVD is a bottleneck in tensor train decomposition; sketching offers a way to accelerate the computation.
method: The authors develop a one-pass sketching algorithm combined with subspace iteration to compute TT approximations, and provide error bounds and robustness analysis.
result: Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
conclusion: The proposed randomized algorithm provides a faster alternative for TT decomposition while maintaining accuracy.

title: Stcc: A Unified Source-Channel Semantic Token Coding Framework For Semantic Communications
authors: Zhicheng Bao, Chen Dong, Sen Wang, Long Liu, Nan Ma, Hao Chen, Xiaodong Xu, Yinqiu Liu, Ping Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (JSCC) has emerged as a promising paradigm for overcoming the ``cliff effect" in wireless communications. However, existing Deep JSCC frameworks operate directly on raw analog data such as image pixels rather than the discrete semantic tokens that foundation models require. Moreover, traditional systems employ fixed, hand-designed constellations that treat all tokens equally, leading to catastrophic random errors under channel noise. In this paper, the Semantic Token Codebook Communication (STCC) is proposed as a unified source-channel semantic token coding framework designed to transmit the discrete semantic tokens of foundation models over noisy channels. The core of STCC is the Semantic Token Codec (STC). It accepts discrete tokens as input, which maintains compatibility with foundation models while employing a residual multiple layer perceptron, i.e., MLP-based encoder that learns geometrically structured constellations optimized with a triple-loss objective. This learned mapping forces the channel topology to align with the semantic embedding space, ensuring that channel noise results in topological errors rather than random corruption. This phenomenon is theoretically and empirically characterized, identifying ``Semantic Drift" in symbolic modalities and ``Structural Distortion" in perceptual modalities, where errors shift predictions to semantically or structurally similar tokens. Extensive experiments demonstrate that STCC significantly outperforms traditional systems in low-SNR regimes, effectively converting channel noise into semantic variations without requiring receiver-side modification.
tldr: Proposes a unified source-channel semantic token coding framework for wireless communications using learned constellations.
motivation: Existing deep JSCC methods operate on raw analog data and treat all tokens equally, leading to catastrophic errors under channel noise.
method: Introduces Semantic Token Codec (STC) with a residual MLP encoder that learns geometrically structured constellations via a triple-loss objective, aligning channel topology with semantic embedding space.
result: STCC significantly outperforms traditional systems in low-SNR regimes, converting channel noise into semantic variations without receiver-side modification.
conclusion: The framework effectively bridges semantic tokens and channel coding, improving robustness in noisy wireless environments.

title: Approximation Properties Of Evolutionary Dynamics In Continuous-Time Finite State Space Games
authors: Pietro Grassi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This thesis studies the convergence of finite-population stochastic evolutionary dynamics to their deterministic mean-field limit in continuous-time finite state space games. We first develop refined ergodic theorems for Markov chains with a single positive-recurrent class, guaranteeing the existence of a unique invariant distribution and almost-sure convergence of time averages. Next, we prove that the mean-field model, described by a system of Lipschitz-continuous ordinary differential equations, admits a unique solution that depends continuously on its initial condition and that constitutes the almost-sure limit for the empirical distributions with fixed policy. Furthermore, we show that every Mixed Stationary Nash Equilibrium of the mean-field game is approximated by a Nash equilibrium of the corresponding [MATH]-player game within an error [MATH] for sufficiently large [MATH]. We finally demonstrate, by Kurtz's theorem, that the empirical state-policy distribution converges in probability to the mean-field trajectory. Numerical simulations conducted in MATLAB confirm the theoretical [MATH] convergence rate in both models across a range of population sizes.
tldr: This thesis studies the convergence of finite-population stochastic evolutionary dynamics to deterministic mean-field limits in continuous-time finite state space games, with applications to Nash equilibrium approximation.
motivation: To rigorously establish the connection between finite-population stochastic evolutionary dynamics and their mean-field approximations in game theory.
method: Uses refined ergodic theorems for Markov chains, Lipschitz ODE analysis, and Kurtz's theorem to prove convergence of empirical distributions to mean-field trajectories.
result: Proves that the mean-field model has a unique solution, that empirical distributions converge almost surely, and that mixed stationary Nash equilibria of the mean-field game approximate those of finite-player games with error O(1/N).
conclusion: The mean-field approximation is valid for large populations, with numerical simulations confirming the theoretical convergence rate.

title: An Entropy-based Framework For Hybrid Coalitions In Game Theory. Part I: Human Arbitration
authors: Jose M. Amigo Salome A. Sepulveda-Fontaine
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Game Theory underpins much of AI and multiagent research, but hybrid Human AI systems require a framework in which execution authority can alternate within a digital environment. We introduce NeoGame Theory, an extension of classical Game Theory for hybrid Human AI coalitions operating under Virtual Nature, the algorithmic analogue of classical (physical) Nature. The framework combines a lexicographic coalition utility with a delegation rule based on the Jensen-Shannon divergence between Human and AI policies. Two thresholds define agreement, contextual, and disagreement regions. In the contextual region, execution follows a scenario specific rule. Apart from the theory, in this paper we develop the first regime, Human arbitration, in which the AI learns by observation and frequency matching while the Human retains final execution authority. We establish the axiomatic basis of the framework and characterize a frequency convergence equilibrium, providing the foundation for later extensions and computational validation.
tldr: This paper proposes NeoGame Theory, an extension of classical game theory for hybrid human-AI coalitions using Jensen-Shannon divergence and a delegation rule.
motivation: Classical game theory does not account for hybrid human-AI systems where execution authority can alternate; a new framework is needed.
method: The framework combines lexicographic coalition utility with a delegation rule based on Jensen-Shannon divergence between human and AI policies, defining agreement, contextual, and disagreement regions.
result: An axiomatic basis is established and a frequency convergence equilibrium is characterized for the human arbitration regime.
conclusion: This work provides a foundation for later extensions and computational validation of hybrid human-AI game theory.

tldr: This paper studies the effect of Ni doping on carrier density and anomalous transport in the heavy-fermion superconductor CeCoIn5 using Hall resistivity measurements.
motivation: To understand how Ni substitution alters the electronic structure and transport properties of CeCoIn5, a prototypical heavy-fermion superconductor.
method: Hall resistivity measurements were performed on single crystals of Ni-doped CeCoIn5 to extract carrier density and anomalous Hall effect contributions.
result: Ni doping changes the carrier density and modifies the anomalous Hall effect, indicating a shift in the electronic band structure and scattering mechanisms.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the doping dependence of electronic properties in heavy-fermion systems, but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Deciphering The Absence Of Charge Density Waves In The V-based Kagome Metal $\mathrm{Cs}{\mathrm{V}}_{6}{\mathrm{Sb}}_{6}$
authors: Rongxiao Du, Yunfan Yang, Wenxin Lv, Junhong Yu, Hang Zhang, Hechang Lei, And Jianbo Hu
abstract:
Author(s): Rongxiao Du, Yunfan Yang, Wenxin Lv, Junhong Yu, Hang Zhang, Hechang Lei, and Jianbo Hu

While charge density waves (CDWs) are a hallmark of the kagome metal [MATH], their absence in the bilayer counterpart [MATH] remains a notable exception, with the underlying mechanism yet to be elucidated. Here, integrat…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245119] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates the absence of charge density waves in the bilayer kagome metal CsV6Sb6 using experimental and theoretical methods.
motivation: Charge density waves are common in kagome metals, but their absence in CsV6Sb6 is puzzling and may reveal new physics.
method: The authors integrate ultrafast spectroscopy, Raman scattering, and first-principles calculations to study the electronic and lattice dynamics.
result: They find that strong interlayer coupling and electronic correlations suppress the CDW instability in the bilayer system.
conclusion: The absence of CDWs in CsV6Sb6 is due to enhanced interlayer interactions and electronic correlations, providing insight into kagome physics.

title: Electronic Coupling Across The In/Si(111) Interface: Quantum Well States And Heavy-hole Subbands In The Si Space-charge Layer
authors: Shinichiro Hatta, Kenta Kuroishi, Tomoka Murata, Mahiro Yamashita, Hiroshi Okuyama, And Tetsuya Aruga

We studied the electronic structure of multilayer indium films grown on Si(111) using angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy. Quantum well state (QWS) bands derived from In [MATH] electrons were observed in the energy range of 0–3.4 eV, and their thickness-dependent energy shifts were well reprodu…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245412] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the electronic structure of indium films on silicon using photoelectron spectroscopy, focusing on quantum well states and heavy-hole subbands.
motivation: To understand the electronic coupling at the In/Si(111) interface and the formation of quantum well states and heavy-hole subbands in the Si space-charge layer.
method: Angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy was used to measure the electronic structure of multilayer indium films on Si(111), and the data were analyzed with theoretical models.
result: Quantum well state bands derived from In sp electrons were observed, and their thickness-dependent energy shifts were reproduced. Heavy-hole subbands in the Si space-charge layer were also identified.
conclusion: The study provides detailed insights into the electronic structure of the In/Si interface, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: General Framework For Twisted Bilayer Photonic Crystal With Interlayer Coupling And Far-field Response
authors: Shupeng Xu, Dun Wang, And Ritesh Agarwal
abstract:
Author(s): Shupeng Xu, Dun Wang, and Ritesh Agarwal

We develop a general theory for twisted bilayer photonic crystals that takes into account both far-field response and near-field coupling. The theory is based on the framework of a generalized Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory for non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. A universal form for interlayer co…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245413] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: Develops a general theory for twisted bilayer photonic crystals using non-Hermitian perturbation theory, focusing on interlayer coupling and far-field response.
motivation: To understand and control the optical properties of twisted bilayer photonic crystals, which are important for photonic device applications.
method: Generalized Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory for non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, incorporating both near-field and far-field coupling.
result: Derives a universal form for interlayer coupling and predicts far-field response features.
conclusion: The framework provides a comprehensive theoretical tool for designing twisted bilayer photonic structures.
